summary: This program defines a general RobotPet class and three specialized versions of it — a cat, a bird, and a dog — each adding its own sound method. One of each is created and asked to speak.

lines.text: The base class holds everything all robot pets share, so the subclasses do not have to repeat it.

lines.code: self.battery = battery  # uses the property setter for validation
lines.text: Assigning to self.battery does not store the value directly; it goes through the setter defined below, so bad values are corrected before they are ever saved.
The property decorator turns the following method into a read-only attribute, so code says pet.battery rather than pet.battery().
The real value lives in _battery, and the leading underscore signals that outside code should leave it alone and use the property instead.
This registers the next method as the code that runs whenever anything assigns to battery.
Negative charge is impossible, so the setter quietly clamps it up to zero instead of storing nonsense.
A battery cannot exceed full, so anything above 100 is capped at 100.
Naming RobotPet in the parentheses makes RobotCat inherit its __init__ and its battery property, so the cat needs no constructor of its own.
This is the cat's own contribution: behaviour that only cats have, added on top of what was inherited.
The method reads self.name even though RobotCat never sets it, which shows the inherited constructor did that work.
The bird inherits the same foundation, showing that one base class can serve any number of subclasses.
The dog is a third subclass, differing from the others only in the sound method it adds.
Creating a RobotCat calls RobotPet's __init__, so all three arguments are handled by inherited code.
Each object keeps its own name, battery, and mood, so the three pets do not interfere with one another.
Each object responds to the method belonging to its own class, which is why the three calls have different names.
